title: How we handle a new ad a client doesn't love

content.job: Standalone written email telling the full exchange and its meaning. No offer or reply prompt; proposed send details require WIA confirmation and publication clearance.
content.body:
I invited specific changes.

I also told them that if they decided they didn't want to use the ads at all, there'd be no hard feelings.

A revision was available. So was choosing not to use those particular ads.

**Our work on an ad shouldn't create an obligation for you to approve it.**

When you hire an advertising team, you're bringing in people with expertise and the capacity to do work you'd otherwise be handling. But you're still the person whose wedding business is being represented to couples.

You can appreciate what the team has contributed and have reservations about the proposed creative. Both can be true in the same conversation.

The owner's reaction gives us something real to respond to, and there should be room for an answer to remain undecided.

Creative review should give the owner a meaningful role in choosing what represents the business. That means being able to request a change, but also being able to decide that a draft isn't the direction they want.

The fact that someone has already made it shouldn't make that answer harder to give.
content.ending:
You know your brand better than anyone. Expert help with your ads should make it easier to say what you really think about a draft, long before anyone decides whether it goes live.

Talk soon,
Whitney

content.title: Your say in a new ad should include the option to decline it.

slides.job: State the promise as an insight about the owner's role in creative approval.
slides.text:
Your say in a new ad should include the option to decline it.

When your ad team sends creative for review,
**a no should be as easy to give as a yes.**
Even when the team has already made it.

slides.job: Begin the story with the team's contribution, without inventing production details.
slides.text:
We'd sent new ads for review.

Our team had made the proposed creative for a client's Meta campaigns.
We sent it over and checked in on our call to hear what they thought.

slides.job: Preserve the tentative nature of the client's response.
slides.text:
Their first reaction was honest.

"I don't think that I love them."
They also said they hadn't finished reviewing them yet.
So this was a starting point, not a final answer.

slides.job: Show Whitney's response, keeping both available options and their actor intact.
slides.text:
Whitney gave them room for either answer.

She invited specific edits.
She also said that if they'd rather not use those ads, that was fine, with no hard feelings either way.

slides.job: Connect the exchange to the established owner's situation.
slides.text:
You might recognize the pull here.

Someone put time into the ad.
Saying you don't love it can feel unkind.
So you approve it and move on, even when it's not how you want couples to see you.

slides.job: State the belief without claiming a documented across-client policy.
slides.text:
The effort behind an ad doesn't decide whether it runs.

You know your venue, your style and your couples.
That judgment belongs in the review, alongside our expertise.
A draft is an offer, and you choose what to do with it.

slides.job: Close on the relationship both management and guided-support readers would want, with no explicit ask.
slides.text:
**We believe your approval is yours to give, never something we're owed.**

We can respect the work our team puts in and still want your candid answer.
Approval only counts when declining was possible.

Whether we manage your ads for you, or we launch your campaigns, then guide you while you run them, the same honesty applies.

The business is yours.
The final say on what couples see should be too.

caption.body:
When you've built a wedding business you're proud of, you notice everything. The photo that doesn't capture your space. The headline that sounds a little generic. The tone that's close to you, but off. And when that shows up in a new ad your team made, it's easy to talk yourself out of saying anything.

A client recently had that kind of reaction to some new ads from us. They weren't sure they loved them, and they hadn't finished their review. I welcomed specific edits and made it clear that not using those ads was a fine answer too.

Our effort on a draft doesn't turn your approval into an obligation. That holds whether we're managing your campaigns or guiding you while you handle your own.

When you can be candid, reviews stop feeling like a test of politeness. You end up with creative you genuinely want in front of couples, and we get feedback we can actually work with.
caption.hook: How easy is it to tell your ad team the truth about a draft?

You can value an agency's expertise and still have a different reaction to a draft.

For a wedding business, that draft is something couples may see as a representation of you. It makes sense for your perspective to remain part of the decision, even when someone else is doing the advertising work.

We believe approval should mean the owner is comfortable choosing the ad.

The effort behind a draft deserves respect, but it doesn't decide whether that draft should be used. A useful creative conversation can hold both things: the team's contribution and the client's freedom to give a candid answer.

slides.job: Close on the relationship both management and guided-support readers would want, with no explicit ask.
slides.text:
Different levels of advertising support can leave room for the same honesty.

That matters whether you want a team managing your campaigns or expert guidance while you run them. The business is still yours. We'd want the conversation to make space for your judgment, including when a particular ad isn't one you want to put forward.

caption.body:
You may want to hand over campaign management, or stay involved in running your ads with expert support. Either way, it matters that you can give a direct answer when something is ready for review.

An owner who knows their wedding business well brings context about how they want couples to see it. That perspective can sit alongside the advertising team's expertise without every draft receiving an automatic yes.

When we share proposed creative, we can leave open both the possibility of adjustments and the possibility of not using it.

Work has been contributed, but the conversation can still allow a choice about what happens next.

For us, that is a useful way to think about creative approval: the owner's reaction belongs in the decision, rather than being something to smooth over so the draft can move forward.
caption.hook: Choosing an advertising partner also means choosing how feedback will feel.
caption.ending: A working relationship should have enough room for a client to be honest without turning that honesty into a disagreement about the team's effort.

content.title: The new ads a client didn't love
content.script:
How would you feel telling your advertising team you didn't love an ad they'd already made?

We recently sent a client some new ads, and they told me they didn't think they loved them. When we send new ads for review, there are a couple of options. If there are specific changes you want, you can tell us. But you can also decide we don't use those ads at all.

We've done the work. That doesn't mean you owe us an approval.

When you know your wedding business well, you have a perspective on how you want it shown to couples. Bringing in an advertising team should leave room for that perspective.

Being able to have that conversation matters. You can appreciate the effort someone has put into an ad and still decide it isn't one you want to use. There should be room to say that without feeling like you're letting the team down.

caption.body:
You know your wedding business better than anyone. You know how you want couples to feel when they come across it, whether that's in a Google search, on your website or scrolling Instagram late at night.

So when your ad team sends over new creative and something feels off, it can be awkward to say so. They've put time into it. You don't want to seem difficult. You might just sign off to keep things moving.

Not long ago, our team sent a client new Meta ads to review. On our call, they said they weren't sure they loved them and hadn't finished looking yet.

I told them specific edits were welcome, and that leaving those ads unused was an option too, with no hard feelings.

It was a small moment, but it says a lot about how a partnership should work. The effort we put into a draft is ours to give. Your approval is yours to decide.

When you can be that honest with the people helping with your ads, reviews get lighter. You stop approving things out of politeness, and what reaches couples is something you actually want representing your business.

content.title: Your yes isn't owed
content.script:
I don't think the work we put into an ad should ever buy us a yes from a client.

Here's what I mean. When you hire a team to run your ads, part of what you're hiring us for is making the creative and sending it over for review. And I get why that can make a no feel rude. Someone sat down and made this thing for you, right?

But you're the one who knows how your venue, your photography or your planning business should look to couples. That call belongs to you.

This came up with a client recently. They weren't sure they loved a few new ads we'd sent, and they hadn't finished reviewing them. I told them edits were welcome, and if they'd rather not use them, that's completely fine. No hard feelings.

Honestly, I'd rather hear that than get a polite approval on an ad you don't love. Your yes only means something when a no was a real option.

That's the kind of working relationship I think every owner deserves with their ad team: one where you can simply tell us what you think.

caption.body:
You open the email, look at the new ad your team created, and something isn't quite right. Maybe the photo isn't the moment you'd choose to show couples. Maybe the words don't sound like the way you talk on a tour or a consultation call. But the team has already done the work, and you'd rather not make things awkward, so you think about approving it anyway.

I believe the effort behind an ad should never turn approval into an obligation.

When a client recently told me they weren't sure they loved some new ads we'd sent, and that they hadn't finished reviewing them, I said two things. Send any specific edits you'd like. And if you'd rather not use those ads, that's fine too.

That's how I want every creative review to feel for the owner on the other side of it. Your perspective on your brand is the reason the review exists in the first place.

When declining is genuinely on the table, saying yes means something. You approve the ads you actually want couples to see, and the conversation about your business gets more honest.
caption.hook: There's a quiet pressure that comes with reviewing work someone made for you.

content.title: The option to pass

caption.body:
You've spent years shaping how couples see your wedding business: the photos you choose, the words on your website, the way you reply to a new inquiry. So when fresh ads arrive for your review and one misses the mark, there's a real tension. The team has contributed its work, and you bring your judgment about how your business should appear to couples.

On a recent call, a client hadn't finished reviewing some new ads from us, and their first reaction was that they didn't think they loved them.

I told them specific edits were welcome, and that leaving those ads unused was a perfectly good answer too.

We believe the work behind a draft is something we bring to the partnership, never a debt you settle with a yes. Your judgment about how your business shows up deserves the final word.

When declining is genuinely possible, feedback gets easier to give. You can say what you'd change, or simply say a direction isn't for you, and the ads that run are ones you're glad to have out there.

So when fresh ads arrive for your review and one misses the mark, there's a real tension. The team has put effort in, and you want to be easy to work with.

That tension came up on a recent call. A client hadn't finished reviewing some new ads from us, and their first reaction was that they didn't think they loved them.

I told them specific edits were welcome, and that leaving those ads unused was a perfectly good answer too.

We believe the work behind a draft is something we bring to the partnership, never a debt you settle with a yes. Your judgment about how your business shows up deserves the final word.

When declining is genuinely possible, feedback gets easier to give. You can say what you'd change, or simply say a direction isn't for you, and the ads that run are ones you're glad to have out there.
changes.before:
When you bring in people to help advertise your wedding business, you're choosing their expertise. You're also entering a working relationship where you need to be able to speak plainly about what feels right for your brand.

A proposed ad can be the place where those two things meet. The team has contributed its work, and you bring your judgment about how your business should appear to couples.

Whitney made room for revisions without making revisions the only acceptable route. Choosing not to move ahead with those particular drafts was also an option.

That response matters because feedback becomes more useful when agreement isn't the assumed destination. An owner can explain what they'd prefer, or simply be honest that a proposed direction isn't one they want to use.

We believe a partnership should be able to accommodate that answer while keeping respect for both the owner's perspective and the team's contribution.

changes.after: -Whitney
changes.before: The relationship we'd want is one where candor belongs in the review, even when the team has already invested effort.
